01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
classification
A category used to organise material.
prescribed
Required or set out by a procedure.
corroboration
Independent evidence supporting a claim.
intrusive
Unnecessarily entering private matters.
confidentiality
The protection of information shared in trust.
contemporaneous
Created at the time of the events described.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The newspaper archive had managed to clarify the classification of the 12 October 2011 item without releasing the correspondence itself. Its surviving catalogue description placed the document among requests or material provided for information about the student travel scheme. The phrase “decision not received” was a staff-generated label, the archivist confirmed; its relationship to the sender's exact language could not be established without examining the underlying document.

Emma relayed the update to Sarah, who initially treated it as disappointing.

“Perhaps it wasn't even a complaint.”

“Perhaps not,” Emma replied. “But a catalogue category isn't a reliable substitute for the writer's intention. It tells us how the newspaper filed the material.”

The temptation was to turn the ambiguous label into an anonymous allegation. Emma resisted. Whatever the item contained, no evidence yet established its author, the status of any application or an actual failure to deliver a decision.

Fiona Bell's subsequent call added a procedural detail from the trust's 2011 office instructions. Staff were expected to prepare decision notices promptly after the selection panel met. The instructions did not define a dispatch deadline, and Fiona could not match the rule to particular completed letters. The appeals folder still awaited inspection; its title disclosed nothing conclusive about whether formal reviews had occurred.

Emma assembled a matrix distinguishing prescribed action, recorded action and verified outcome. The notice template and office guidance belonged in the first category. Fiona's preliminary description of dispatch entries offered limited evidence for the second. Nothing she had received yet established that any named applicant had obtained, understood or been denied the opportunity to request review.

Sarah proposed contacting former applicants directly. The suggestion was sensible in principle, but the route mattered. Requesting personal details from the trust's historical files would be intrusive, and a journalist's interest in a case did not erase the privacy of people who had once applied for financial support.

They decided instead to invite voluntary contact through the newspaper. Emma drafted an appeal to readers asking for first-hand experiences of the 2011 travel programme. On rereading it, she found a sentence that asked whether applicants had been wrongly refused assistance. It presumed a conclusion that her documents did not justify.

She replaced it with neutral questions: had readers applied, assisted someone with an application, received a decision notice or been informed about the review procedure? She made clear that contacting the newsroom would not automatically lead to publication. The newsroom would need to explain any confidentiality limits and obtain permission before sharing identifying material.

It was an unglamorous intervention, and one that carried risks of its own. People might misremember events from fifteen years earlier; a former applicant might confuse selection with payment; someone with an unrelated grievance might find the wording suggestive. Emma added a verification plan: record when an account was given, distinguish recollection from contemporaneous documents and seek independent corroboration where possible.

She thought briefly of Claire's warning that journalists sometimes asked the wrong questions. In 2011 Emma had allowed a tidy interpretation to replace a careful inquiry. This time she was trying to design a question that could be answered without first accepting her assumptions.

She sent the draft to Sarah for editorial approval. No witness had yet come forward, and no publication had been authorised. Still, the next stage of the investigation was taking shape: not the revelation of a culprit, but the creation of a way for the people affected to speak on their own terms.
